extracted.intended_audience: DHS officials, consular and immigration officers, immigration attorneys, advocacy organizations, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Federal rulemaking/preamble describing standards, definitions, evidentiary frameworks, statutory requirements, and regulatory history for determining when an alien is inadmissible as a "public charge." Intended to guide adjudicators and inform public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether an alien is likely at any time to become a public charge, consular officers and immigration officers must, at a minimum, consider the alien's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited to INA sec. 212(a)(4)(B)(i). These five factors are mandatory baseline considerations for public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support (Section 213A) — consideration and requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The consular officer or immigration officer may consider any Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA submitted on the alien's behalf; most family-based immigrants and some employment-based immigrants must submit a sufficient Affidavit of Support to avoid being found inadmissible as likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit of Support is legally enforceable (Section 213A) and provides a mechanism for benefit-granting agencies to seek reimbursement; filing a sufficient affidavit is required for many family-based and certain employment-based applicants (see INA sec. 212(a)(4)(C) and (D)). Congress permitted but did not require officers to consider the affidavit as a factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge determinations should be made based on the totality of the alien's circumstances; the existence or absence of a particular factor should never be the sole criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically articulated in administrative decisions and regulations (e.g., 8 CFR 245a.3), and reiterated in DHS rulemaking: adjudicators must weigh multiple factors prospectively rather than relying on a single element.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1999 INS definition: primary dependence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: INS (1999 NPRM/Interim Field Guidance) defined 'public charge' to mean an alien who is likely to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence, as demonstrated by either (i) the receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance or (ii) institutionalization for long-term care at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INS stated that non-cash benefits and supplemental/special-purpose cash benefits should not be considered under the primary-dependence framing; guidance letters from HHS/SSA/USDA influenced but did not bind INS's interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 Final Rule definition: 12-in-36 months aggregate test
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined 'public charge' to mean 'an alien who receives one or more public benefits ... for more than 12 months in the aggregate within any 36-month period' (counts receipt of two benefits in one month as two months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2019 rule also defined the term 'public benefit' to include specific enumerated programs (Federal, State, local, or Tribal cash assistance for income maintenance (other than tax credits), SNAP, most forms of Medicaid, Section 8 HCV, Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance, and certain other subsidized housing). The rule created an evidentiary framework with listed positive/negative and 'heavily weighted' factors and used Form I-944 to collect information.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 Final Rule evidentiary framework (positive/negative/heavily weighted factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2019 Final Rule listed negative and positive factors (and designated some as 'heavily weighted') for officers to consider in the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS indicated that, apart from lack of required Affidavit of Support, the presence of a single positive or negative factor, or a single heavily weighted factor, would never alone create a presumption of inadmissibility; officers should use the factors as guidelines within a totality analysis. Form I-944 collected evidence relevant to these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 Final Rule nonimmigrant extension/change-of-status bar
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2019 Final Rule rendered certain nonimmigrants ineligible for extension of stay or change of status if they received one or more public benefits (as defined by the rule) for more than 12 months in the aggregate within any 36-month period since obtaining the nonimmigrant status they wished to extend or change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision applied to certain nonimmigrants and was separate from admission/adjustment public charge inadmissibility; it extended effect of the benefits-counting rule to change/extension contexts under the 2019 rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2022 Final Rule narrow primary-dependence definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2022 Final Rule defined public charge more narrowly than 2019: as likely at any time to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence, demonstrated by either the receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2022 Rule excluded mandatory consideration of many supplemental public benefits that did not represent primary dependence, aligning more closely with the 1999 Interim Field Guidance. It provided key definitions for 'public cash assistance for income maintenance,' 'long-term institutionalization at government expense,' 'receipt,' 'government,' and 'household.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 2022 Final Rule constrained factor list (seven factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2022 Final Rule constrained public charge inadmissibility determinations to seven factors: (1) the five statutory factors (age; health; family status; assets/resources/financial status; education and skills), (2) the Affidavit of Support under section 213A where required, and (3) current and/or past receipt of TANF; SSI; State/Tribal/territorial/local cash benefit programs for income maintenance; and long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike 2019, the 2022 Rule did not designate 'heavily weighted' positive or negative factors; it limited both the scope of benefits considered and the number of factors officers may use in the totality assessment. The rule applied only to admissions and adjustments of status (not to nonimmigrant change/extensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bright-line prohibition on considering dependents' receipt of benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2022 Final Rule stated a bright-line rule prohibiting consideration of the receipt of public benefits by an alien's dependents (e.g., a U.S. citizen child in a mixed-status household) in a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicitly prevents officers from treating dependent family members' benefit receipt as an adverse factor against the alien applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRWORA definitions and benefit-category distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: PRWORA defined 'Federal public benefit' broadly (grants, contracts, loans, licenses, retirement, welfare, health, disability, public/assisted housing, postsecondary education, food assistance, unemployment benefits, and other similar benefits) and established categories: 'specified Federal programs,' 'Federal means-tested public benefits,' and 'designated Federal programs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRWORA also created a policy of self-sufficiency, set eligibility timing (qualified aliens generally eligible for Federal means-tested benefits after 5 years), and enumerated exceptions (emergency medical assistance, short-term in-kind disaster relief, public health assistance related to immunizations and communicable diseases). States may independently determine eligibility for certain programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for certain aliens and programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of aliens are exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility, and Congress created exceptions allowing eligibility for some benefits (e.g., emergency medical treatment, short-term in-kind emergency disaster relief, immunizations and treatment of communicable diseases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation and later rules list statutory exemptions, waivers, and categories (e.g., refugees, asylees, certain trafficking victims, Cuban/Haitian entrants, certain parolees). The 2022 Final Rule also listed statutory exemptions and waivers at 8 CFR 212.23.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt of public benefits may be an adverse factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some benefits are permissible for certain aliens, Congress (except in limited circumstances) did not prohibit DHS from considering the receipt of such benefits in public charge inadmissibility determinations; consequently, receipt of public benefits can be properly considered an adverse factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The weight of such evidence depends on context, statutory/regulatory definitions, and the totality of circumstances; historical practice and legislative amendments reflect that past receipt may be relevant in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer discretion and prospective/subjective nature of determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory phrase 'in the opinion of' (e.g., 'in the opinion of the consular officer or immigration officer') signals that public charge determinations are discretionary and necessarily subjective because they are prospective evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators must exercise judgment when forecasting future likelihood of becoming a public charge, guided by statutory/regulatory factors and any applicable evidentiary rules and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary collection mechanisms (Form I-944 and Form I-485 information)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS used Form I-944 (Declaration of Self Sufficiency) in the 2019 Final Rule to collect information relevant to the regulatory approach; the 2022 Final Rule required a different information collection incorporated into Form I-485 for adjustment cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of information collection reflects the rule's scope and evidentiary expectations; forms gather data on income, assets, benefit receipt, health, education, and other statutory factors to inform the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical/legislative context and agency policy goals in implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS may consider statutory policy goals (e.g., PRWORA's self-sufficiency policy), congressional intent in IIRIRA, and administrative goals such as clarity, fairness, and administrability when implementing the public charge ground of inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory formulations (1999, 2019, 2022, and the present NPRM) have differed based on competing interpretations of statutory text and policy priorities; the NPRM asserts prior rules were overly restrictive and proposes rescission to align with Executive Order and congressional intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of waivers and public charge bonds under INA sec. 213
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 213 of the INA, the Secretary has discretion to admit into the United States an alien determined inadmissible only on public charge grounds upon the giving of a suitable and proper bond or undertaking approved by the Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public charge bond is a statutory mechanism to mitigate inadmissibility in some cases; rules and agency discretion govern when such bonds may be accepted.
